bull_thesis:
Reddit is one of the very few businesses of any size that combines hyper-growth with real profitability and needs almost no capital to do it. In the June 2026 quarter revenue grew 61% to $805 million, the eighth consecutive quarter above 60%; gross margin (revenue left after the direct cost of delivering it) was 91.3%; operating margin more than doubled from 13.6% a year earlier to 28.8%; and capital spending was $1.1 million against that $805 million of revenue. Free cash flow (cash from operations after capital spending) was $1.02 billion over the last twelve months, up from roughly $434 million a year earlier. The company holds $2.79 billion of cash and short-term investments against $20.9 million of total debt, all of it capitalized leases, verified on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet. Management guided the September quarter to $860-870 million of revenue, 47-49% growth, with an adjusted profit margin of 45% at the midpoint - a guide that came in above what the street expected, from a team that has beaten its own numbers in six of the last seven quarters and that hit the 40% margin target it publicly set at its 2024 listing.

The core of the bull case is that the revenue engine has already proven it does not depend on the traffic that just got worse. In the very quarter Reddit told investors that search referrals were choppy, advertising revenue still grew 64% to $762 million, conversion volume grew over 100%, active advertisers grew over 70%, and the automated Reddit Max advertising product saw its advertiser count grow over 60% in a single quarter with revenue up over 150%. Management's own framing - that a logged-in app user is worth a multiple of a search visitor - is arithmetically supported by what happened: the low-value users left and revenue accelerated in absolute dollars anyway. On top of that, management said in October 2025 that Reddit's ad load is 'much lower than our peers' and that raising it 'is not a core part of our strategy', which means the most obvious monetization lever has not even been pulled yet.

There is a second, unpriced asset: the corpus. Twenty years and more than 25 billion posts and comments, generating what the company describes as a Wikipedia's worth of new content every month, and the most-cited domain in AI answers across models. Today that asset produces almost nothing - 'Other Revenue' was $140 million of $2.2 billion in fiscal 2025 and roughly $43 million in the June quarter. Reported negotiations with Google in late July 2026 over renewing a licensing agreement worth roughly $60 million a year, with Reddit reportedly seeking usage-based fees, are the first sign that this could be repriced from a rounding error to a real line. It is optionality, not a base case, but it is free at the current price.

Finally, capital allocation is genuinely shareholder-friendly and verified rather than promised: $234.6 million of stock was repurchased in the June quarter under the $1 billion programme announced in February 2026, leaving roughly $760 million authorized and now available at a price a third lower. That buyback is already large enough that the diluted share count has fallen from 202.9 million to 202.0 million over three quarters, meaning stock-based pay is being fully absorbed.

The conditions the bull case depends on: (1) advertising revenue per user keeps expanding fast enough to cover flat-to-declining U.S. daily users for at least four more quarters; (2) the direct-and-app engagement work, which management says lifted new app-user retention 50% year over year on a relative basis, keeps compounding; (3) the Google licensing renewal lands at flat or better rather than being lost; and (4) the market is willing to pay a growth multiple again once a quarter arrives showing U.S. daily users back in sequential growth.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Reddit is a bad business. It is that the front door belongs to somebody else, and the price still assumes it does not.

In the June 2026 quarter, U.S. daily unique users fell to 53.2 million from 53.5 million - the first sequential decline in five quarters - and management conceded that search referrals were 'choppy' and 'more volatile later in the quarter' while admitting 'our visibility in referral traffic remains low'. The cause is structural, not cyclical: Google's AI Overviews answer questions on the search page instead of sending the click onward. Comparable publishers have lost between roughly a quarter and 85% of their search traffic to the same force. Reddit's own chief executive went public the same day arguing that AI Overviews 'has yet to make a similar level of positive impact' as the ten blue links. That is a company complaining about its distribution channel, which is what companies do when they cannot change it.

The forensic record here is damning on judgement. Analysts asked about exactly this risk in four consecutive calls. In July 2025 management answered that it was 'a net opportunity for us'. In April 2026, asked directly about Google's algorithm change, Steve Huffman said 'these things are business as usual for us... They almost never stand out on our traffic long term.' One quarter later it was the reason the stock fell 21% in a session. Management was wrong for a year about the single most important input to the business, and no analyst has yet forced them to say how many quarters of revenue-per-user expansion remain.

The arithmetic is the real problem. Revenue grew 61% while global daily users grew roughly 18% and U.S. daily users shrank. All of the outperformance is revenue per user, and revenue per user has a ceiling: ad load, ad pricing and funnel mix are finite levers, whereas users are not. Once that gap closes, revenue growth converges toward user growth, which is currently about zero in the company's most valuable market. Management's response has been to reframe rather than to fix - 'we're not building for drive-by traffic' is a re-definition of success delivered after the miss - and to inflate the goal, moving from '100 million daily U.S. users' in April 2026 to '1 billion daily users globally and 100 million in the U.S.' in July 2026, in the quarter the U.S. base went backwards. Undated aspirations of that size are a tell, not a plan.

The valuation does not yet compensate. Even after a 21% single-day fall and a roughly 50% decline from the $282.95 high, the shares change hands at about nine times enterprise value to trailing revenue (enterprise value being market value plus debt less cash), roughly twenty times the 2027 consensus earnings estimate of $6.95 a share, and about twenty-eight times trailing free cash flow. Meta, growing about 20%, trades near twenty-one times trailing earnings; Pinterest, growing about 15%, trades near 3.6 times enterprise value to revenue. Reddit is still the most expensive name in its peer group on an absolute basis. If growth decelerates from 61% to 47% to the high twenties over the next 18 months - which is precisely the path the current guide starts - the multiple compresses at the same time the numerator slows, and those two things multiply.

Secondary risks. Stock-based pay of $338 million over the last twelve months is 12% of revenue and turns $1.02 billion of reported free cash flow into roughly $681 million of genuinely economic cash flow; the buyback offsets the dilution but at the cost of the cash it is spending. Not one insider has bought a share on the open market against 66 sales totalling 190,308 shares. And the Google licensing negotiation cuts both ways: Reddit is reportedly considering restricting Google's AI access, which would be a confrontation with the counterparty that is simultaneously its largest source of traffic and a $60-million-a-year customer.

What would confirm the bear case: a second consecutive sequential decline in U.S. daily users at the October 2026 print; the September-quarter revenue landing at or below the $860 million low end rather than beating it as the last six quarters did; the Google agreement lapsing without replacement; or advertising revenue growth breaking below 45% year over year.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is subtler than usual, because the market has just moved a very long way in one day and is no longer obviously wrong.

The street's remaining error is the price target, not the direction. Sixteen analysts published targets averaging $206 over the last quarter, and the four published the morning after the fall clustered at $185-221 - Deutsche Bank $200, Wedbush $221, Oppenheimer $200, Baird's Colin Sebastian $185. Only one analyst, Rohit Kulkarni at $145 on 3 August, has actually re-underwritten the business at the new information. Those $200-plus targets require Reddit to compound revenue above 30% into 2028 while U.S. daily users are flat. The 2027 consensus of $4.40 billion in revenue and $6.95 a share of earnings, from 23 to 26 analysts, embeds exactly that. We think the revenue-per-user lever - ad load, pricing, funnel mix, automation - carries the company for another four to six quarters and then converges toward user growth, which in the United States is currently zero. Our base case of $154 is deliberately 25% below the street.

The street's other error runs the opposite way, and it is why this is not a pass. The one-day fall priced Reddit as though the advertising engine depends on search referrals. It does not, and the June quarter is the proof: advertising revenue grew 64% to $762 million in the very quarter referrals turned choppy, conversion volume grew over 100%, and active advertisers grew over 70%. The bear reading extrapolates a user metric into a revenue metric that has already demonstrated its independence. So the market is now roughly right in aggregate and wrong in both directions at once - too optimistic on the terminal growth rate, too pessimistic on the near-term revenue line.

The genuinely unexamined item is the corpus. 'Other Revenue' - data licensing plus premium subscriptions - was $140 million of $2.2 billion in fiscal 2025 and roughly $43 million in the June quarter. Almost no sell-side model gives it a separate multiple. If the reported push for usage-based licensing terms succeeds, that line reprices from a rounding error to something worth several dollars a share. Nobody is paid to be wrong about it, so nobody models it.
forcing_function:
For a business with stable and growing earnings power, the question is what makes the market re-rate it. There are three candidates and only one of them carries a date.

The dated one is the third-quarter report, expected in late October 2026 (the screener puts the next report roughly 87 days out). This is the forcing function that matters, and it works in both directions. If U.S. daily users return to sequential growth from the 53.2 million June base - which is what management's product work on app conversion, onboarding and post-success is aimed at, and where they claim new app-user retention improved 50% year over year on a relative basis - then the entire bear premise is falsified in a single line of a shareholder letter and the growth multiple comes back fast. If users decline again, the deceleration story is confirmed and the stock revisits the bear case. Nothing else the company can say between now and then resolves it.

The undated one is the Google licensing renewal. A usage-based agreement announced at a materially higher figure would convert 'Other Revenue' from a rounding error into a separately-valued asset and would validate the scarcity argument that underpins the top half of our range. Reddit has no obligation to disclose the outcome on any schedule, and the talks were reported by third parties rather than by the company, so this could resolve at any moment or drift for a year.

The continuous one is the buyback. Roughly $760 million remains authorized and the company is executing it - a visibly accelerated repurchase disclosed at the October report, funded from a $2.79 billion cash pile, would be management voting with the balance sheet at a price it clearly regards as wrong. That is not a re-rating event by itself, but it changes the supply-demand balance every day it runs.
valley_of_death:
There is no cash-flow valley here and that needs saying plainly, because the risk is entirely to the multiple rather than to solvency. Reddit generated $1.02 billion of free cash flow over the last twelve months, spends about $1.1 million a quarter on capital equipment, holds $2.79 billion of cash and short-term investments, and carries $20.9 million of total debt - all of it capitalized leases, with no maturity wall of any kind. The company could stop growing entirely and still be comfortably profitable.

The risky window (the months just ahead) is a disclosure window, not a funding one, and it has three specific dates.

First and most important, the third-quarter report expected in late October 2026. This is the print that decides the thesis. A second consecutive sequential decline in U.S. daily users, against 53.2 million in June, would confirm that the referral loss is compounding rather than a one-quarter air pocket, and would take the stock toward the low end of our range. Note also that the September-quarter guide of $860-870 million represents 47-49% growth, down from 61% - the deceleration is already scheduled, and the market will see the second derivative before it sees anything good.

Second, the Google licensing renewal, which is undated. A lapse without replacement removes roughly $60 million of near-100%-margin revenue - immaterial to earnings, but severely damaging to the 'scarce corpus' narrative that supports the premium half of the multiple. A confrontation in which Reddit actually restricts Google's access is more dangerous still, because Google is simultaneously the counterparty and the traffic source.

Third, the market regime itself. The current read has investor cash allocations at a formal sell signal with positioning full, and the tape has been punishing soft guides and heavy spend - Netflix went to a fifty-two-week low on a light quarterly guide in the same season. Negative surprises are travelling much further than positive ones right now, which is exactly what Reddit experienced: a beat-and-raise met with a 21% fall. In that regime, a disappointing October print does not produce a 10% move; it produces another 20% one.

One further caution on the read-across: the force driving Reddit's outcome - generative-AI answer engines absorbing web traffic - is the same shared driver moving every publisher and content name, and it sits adjacent to the AI-capex factor the book is already exposed to. This is not an independent resolution driver, and it should be sized accordingly.
positioning_washout:
The forced-selling pressure has largely already happened, and that is the constructive part of the setup.

On 31 July 2026 Reddit fell 20.99% to $140.67 on 29.1 million shares - the worst single session since the 2024 listing, on volume many multiples of normal. The shares now sit 50% below the $282.95 fifty-two-week high, 22% below the 200-day average, and just 13% up off the fifty-two-week low of $119.27. A move of that size on that volume is momentum funds and growth mandates liquidating mechanically, not considered opinion. Reddit had been a momentum holding - it was carrying a strong momentum classification from ranking services days before the fall - and momentum ownership unwinds violently and completely.

What has not yet happened is the sell-side capitulation. Fifteen to sixteen analysts still carry targets averaging above $200; only one has cut to near the current price. Until those targets come down, there is a second, slower wave of downgrades still to run, and each one is a fresh headline for holders who bought on the old thesis. That is a reason to wait rather than a reason to buy the first flush.

The offsetting mechanical buyer is real and dated. Roughly $760 million of the $1 billion buyback authorized on 5 February 2026 remains, and the company just demonstrated it will use it - $234.6 million in the June quarter alone, verified in the cash-flow statement filed 31 July 2026. At $140 that remaining authorization is about 2.7% of the shares outstanding, and the company has $2.79 billion of cash with which to accelerate it. If management steps up repurchases into this fall, that is the single most informative signal available before October, and it is the one to watch.

The discouraging counterweight: not one insider has bought a share on the open market, against 66 sales totalling 190,308 shares. Corporate confidence is being expressed with the company's cash; personal confidence is not being expressed at all.
moderator_conclusion:
Reddit is an excellent business that has fallen from expensive to fair, and the honest answer is to wait rather than to buy.

Start with what is not in dispute. The June 2026 quarter delivered $805 million of revenue, up 61% - the eighth straight quarter above 60% - at a 91.3% gross margin, with operating margin more than doubling year over year to 28.8% and capital spending of $1.1 million. Free cash flow is $1.02 billion over the last twelve months. The balance sheet holds $2.79 billion of cash and short-term investments against $20.9 million of debt, all capitalized leases. The September-quarter guide of $860-870 million at a 45% adjusted margin came in above what the street expected. Management set a margin target at its 2024 listing, hit it, and has beaten its own numbers in six of the last seven quarters. On the forensic evidence this is a credible team running a genuinely rare business, and they told investors the bad news themselves rather than waiting to be caught.

Now the crack. U.S. daily users fell sequentially for the first time in five quarters, to 53.2 million from 53.5 million, and management conceded search referrals were choppy while admitting their visibility into that traffic is low. The cause is structural: AI answer engines are absorbing the clicks that used to arrive as links. Analysts asked about this risk in four consecutive calls and were told in April 2026 that it was 'business as usual' and that such changes 'almost never stand out on our traffic long term'. That judgement was wrong within one quarter, and it is the clearest debit in the file.

The reason this is not a pass is that the revenue engine has already shown it does not depend on that traffic - advertising grew 64% in the very quarter referrals turned choppy. The reason it is not a purchase is arithmetic. Revenue grew 61% while global users grew about 18% and U.S. users shrank; all of the outperformance is revenue per user, and revenue per user has a ceiling that users do not. Our sum-of-the-parts lands at about $154 a share - advertising at 7.5 times forward revenue, licensing at 8 times, plus $13.69 a share of verified net cash - against a $140.67 price. Roughly 10% of upside to fair value with a credible path to $96 if the October print shows a second sequential user decline is the wrong shape of trade, and there is no structural floor: the net cash is solvency comfort, not price support.

The market regime sharpens the point. Positioning is full, the tape is punishing soft guides far harder than it rewards beats, and Reddit just took a 21% single-day hit on a beat-and-raise. Fifteen analysts still carry targets above $200 and have not yet cut - there is a second wave of downgrades still to come. Buying the first flush in that environment is how you find the second one.

The catalyst picture is soft and non-binding rather than firm. The reported Google licensing renewal - roughly $60 million a year, with Reddit said to be seeking usage-based terms and weighing restricting AI access - has no date, no contractual payout and depends entirely on the counterparty. In this book that is neither a plus nor a penalty, and the residual value case has to stand alone. It stands, but not cheaply.

So: wait for the wash-out, and name it. Two triggers would move this to a purchase. Either the price reaches roughly $115 - about 6.5 times forward advertising revenue plus net cash, sixteen times the 2027 consensus earnings estimate, and near the fifty-two-week low - at which point the skew inverts and the bear case is largely paid for. Or the October 2026 third-quarter report shows U.S. daily users back in sequential growth, which falsifies the bear premise outright and justifies paying up. Until one of those two things happens, this is a high-quality franchise at a fair price with an unfavorable skew, and there is no reward for being early.

On durability: the moat is a real network effect - roughly 100,000 communities, 25 billion accumulated posts and comments, and an unpaid moderator base nobody can buy - but it is narrow rather than wide, because the customer arrives through a door Google owns and the switching cost for a casual visitor is zero. Returns and margins are high and rising, so the monetization side is strengthening; the distribution side is weakening. Net it out and the moat is stable. The structural threat from generative-AI displacement of web traffic is material and real, but not terminal: 130 million direct daily users, an app, and an 80-million-weekly-user search product of its own are a genuine buffer that a newspaper does not have.
sop_breakdown: Base case, per diluted share on 202.0 million shares, in US dollars. Advertising: forward twelve-month revenue of roughly $3.58 billion at 7.5 times revenue = $26.85 billion. That multiple is a modest premium to Meta's live 6.7 times enterprise value to revenue, which is defensible for a business growing two-and-a-half times as fast, at a nine-point-higher gross margin, with roughly one-seventieth the capital intensity - and it already embeds growth decelerating from 61% today toward the mid-twenties over the next two years. Data licensing and other revenue: $190 million forward at 8 times = $1.52 billion, splitting the difference between a lapsed Google agreement and a usage-based repricing. Net cash overlay: $2.77 billion, verified on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet ($2.79 billion of cash and short-term investments against $20.9 million of total debt, all capitalized leases) - about $13.69 per share. Total equity value $31.1 billion, or approximately $154 per share. Cross-check on earnings power: $154 is about 22 times the 2027 consensus earnings estimate of $6.95 a share and roughly 30 times our estimate of this year's earnings - reasonable for the growth and margin profile, and deliberately below the $207 street consensus target because that target embeds continued 30%-plus growth, which is exactly what the referral-traffic crack calls into question.
risk_reward: Poor, and that is the whole call. The base-case fair value of $154 sits only modestly above the $140.67 price, while the adverse case of $96 sits far below it - the distance down to the bear is roughly three times the distance up to fair value. The favorable case of $212 is worth real money, but it requires a licensing repricing and a return to sequential U.S. user growth, neither of which is dated or contracted. There is no structural floor beneath this stock: the $13.69 a share of net cash is a solvency comfort, not a price support, and the fifty-two-week low of $119.27 is a chart level, not a floor. A quality franchise at a fair price with an unfavorable skew is a watchlist name, not a purchase.
peer_comps_note:
The peer file's verdict of 'rich versus peers' rests on a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 41.6 times, and that number is built on a stale denominator - it uses fiscal 2025 free cash flow of roughly $684 million rather than the $1.02 billion the company has actually generated over the last twelve months. On current figures the multiple is about 28 times, not 42. That correction matters, and it changes the conclusion less than you would hope.

Against live peer marks rather than remembered ones: Meta currently trades at 6.7 times enterprise value to revenue and about 21 times trailing earnings, growing roughly 20%, with an 82% gross margin and a very large capital-spending bill. Pinterest trades at about 3.6 times enterprise value to revenue and 50 times trailing earnings, growing roughly 15%. Snap trades at 1.8 times revenue and does not earn money. Reddit, after the fall, trades at roughly 9.2 times enterprise value to trailing revenue and about 33 times trailing earnings.

So Reddit is still the most expensive name in the group on an absolute basis - the peer file's headline verdict survives. But adjusted for growth it is now the cheapest: about 0.15 times enterprise-value-to-revenue per point of growth, against 0.24 for Pinterest and 0.34 for Meta. Reddit also carries the best gross margin in the group at 91% and by far the lowest capital intensity. On the forward earnings estimate of $6.95 a share for 2027, Reddit at 20 times is close to Meta's trailing 21 times for two to three times the growth rate.

The honest reading is that Reddit has de-rated from expensive to defensible, not to cheap - and that the peer gap is not idiosyncratic edge. Every name here is exposed to the same unresolved driver: how much traffic and advertising value generative-AI answer engines take out of the open web. That is a shared sector factor, and it should not be credited as name-specific opportunity.
interrogator_dossier:
# Reddit, Inc. (RDDT) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-08-03 · **Price used:** $140.67 (US dollars, NYSE, 2026-07-31 close — the day the stock fell 21%)
**Transcripts examined:** Q2 2025 (2025-07-31) · Q3 2025 (2025-10-30) · Q4/FY 2025 (2026-02-05) · Q1 2026 (2026-04-30) · Q2 2026 (2026-07-30)

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across five calls, Reddit's story has changed shape in a way that is easy to miss because the revenue line never stopped accelerating.

**Mid-2025 — "we control our own destiny."** In the July 2025 call, Steve Huffman framed Reddit as the beneficiary of the artificial-intelligence wave rather than its victim. His three priorities were concrete and product-led: fix the core experience, turn Reddit into a search destination, and expand internationally. He simultaneously *dropped* an initiative — "we are deprioritizing a few initiatives, including our work on the user economy" — the first sign that the company would narrow rather than broaden. The AI framing was almost triumphant: Reddit was "the #1 most cited domain for AI across all models," and "you can't have artificial intelligence without actual intelligence."

**Late 2025 — the profitability proof.** The October 2025 call was the victory lap. Reddit hit the 40% adjusted profit margin target it had set at its 2024 initial public offering, "a profitability goal we set at our IPO just last year," and claimed the number-three most-visited site in the United States. The tone was expansive: publishers, moderators, video, international.

**Early 2026 — the goal gets bigger while the disclosure gets smaller.** Two things happened on the February 2026 call that only look important in hindsight. First, management announced it would "phase out reporting on logged-in and logged-out later this year" — retiring a user-quality disclosure. Second, they announced a $1 billion share-repurchase programme, the first capital-return commitment in the company's life. The April 2026 call raised the ambition to a hard number: "Our goal is to reach 100 million daily U.S. users."

**Mid-2026 — the funnel cracks and the story reframes.** The July 2026 call is the pivot. The 100-million-U.S. goal became "1 billion daily users globally and 100 million in the U.S." — a bigger number attached to a base that had just gone backwards. And for the first time, management led *into* bad news rather than around it: "Search referrals were choppy in the quarter and traffic was more volatile later in the quarter," followed by the defensive reframe, "we're not building for drive-by traffic. We're building a daily destination." Huffman went further in public the same day, telling CNBC that Google's AI Overviews "has yet to make a similar level of positive impact" as the old ten blue links.

**The arc in one line:** the monetization story has strengthened every single quarter; the *distribution* story quietly inverted from "AI makes Reddit more valuable" (2025) to "AI is taking our traffic and we are building around it" (2026).

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where stated | What the numbers say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Eighth consecutive quarter of over 60% revenue growth" | Q2 2026 | Revenue by quarter: $499.6M → $584.9M → $725.6M → $663.4M → $804.9M. Q2 2026 grew 61% year over year. Exactly true. | **Corroborated** |
| Industry-leading gross margins "over 90%" | Q1 2026 | Gross margin: 90.8% (Q2 2025), 91.0%, 91.9%, 91.5%, 91.3% (Q2 2026). Genuinely best-in-class and stable at the top. | **Corroborated** |
| "This was our most profitable quarter yet" (repeatedly) | Q2 2025 onward | Operating margin ran 13.6% → 23.7% → 31.9% → 27.6% → 28.8%. Net income $89.3M → $252.8M over four quarters. Diluted earnings per share $0.48 → $1.25. | **Corroborated, and understated** |
| "Capital expenditures remained low as $1 million" | Q1 2026 | Capital spending was $1.09M in Q1 2026 and $1.13M in Q2 2026 against $805M of quarterly revenue. This is close to a capital-free business. | **Corroborated** |
| "Record cash flow of more than $300 million" | Q1 2026 | Free cash flow (cash from operations minus capital spending): $311.2M in Q1 2026. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is $1.019 billion, up from roughly $434M a year earlier. | **Corroborated** |
| Incremental margins "in the high 50s, low 60s" | Q2 2026 (CFO Vollero) | Revenue rose $305M year over year in Q2 2026; operating income rose $164M. That is a 54% incremental margin — close to, slightly below, the claim. | **Corroborated with a small stretch** |
| $1 billion share repurchase — "a testament to our growth" | Q4 2025 | Verified in the cash-flow statement filed 2026-07-31: $5.0M repurchased in Q1 2026, then **$234.6M in Q2 2026**. Roughly $760M of authorization remains. Diluted share count actually *fell* from 202.9M to 202.0M over three quarters. | **Corroborated — the buyback is real and is fully absorbing dilution** |
| "Reddit now reaches over half a billion people, including more than 130 million daily" | Q2 2026 | True globally. But the number management did not say aloud on the call — it sits in the shareholder letter — is that **U.S. daily uniques fell to 53.2 million from 53.5 million**, the first sequential decline in five quarters. | **Technically true, materially incomplete** |
| "Our goal is to reach 100 million daily U.S. users" | Q1 2026, restated bigger in Q2 2026 | The base moved from 53.5M to 53.2M in the very quarter the goal was expanded to a billion globally. No dated path was given in any call. | **Aspiration, not guidance** |

**The single most important divergence.** The narrative and the financials are pointing in opposite directions on *user acquisition*, and in the same direction on *user monetization*. Revenue per user is doing all of the work: total revenue grew 61% while global daily users grew roughly 18%. That is a wonderful thing while it lasts and a dangerous thing to extrapolate, because average revenue per user is the one line that has a ceiling. Management themselves said in Q3 2025 that raising ad load "is not a core part of our strategy" and that Reddit's ad load is "much lower than our peers" — which is the bull's headroom argument and the bear's reminder that the lever is finite.

**Where the story is poorer than the trajectory justifies.** Nowhere on the profit line. Reddit has earned the right to its financial claims.

**Where the story is richer than the trajectory justifies.** The user story. "Everyone belongs on Reddit" and "1 billion daily users" are aspiration language attached to a U.S. base that shrank sequentially and a top-of-funnel that management concedes they cannot see clearly: "our visibility in referral traffic remains low."

**One accounting caveat the enthusiasm skips.** Stock-based compensation ran $338M over the last twelve months — about 12% of revenue. Free cash flow of $1.019 billion becomes roughly $681M once you charge that as the real cost it is. The saving grace, and it is a genuine one, is that the buyback is now large enough that the diluted share count is falling anyway.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising on the business, Declining on the funnel — a split that first appeared in Q2 2026.**

- **Q2 2025 — expansive, offensive.** "Reddit has a once-in-a-generation opportunity." "We control our own destiny." Marketing spend framed as an accelerator.
- **Q3 2025 — confident and specific.** "We achieved a targeted adjusted EBITDA margin of 40%, which was a profitability goal we set at our IPO." Naming a target and hitting it is the strongest confidence signal in the whole set.
- **Q4 2025 — celebratory, plus a capital-allocation flex.** "2025 was a breakout year." The $1 billion buyback announcement is management putting money where the narrative is.
- **Q1 2026 — the first self-critical note.** "I believe our previous ways of working yielded the best results we were capable of, but not the results we aspire to." That is an unusually candid admission that the product organization was underperforming, paired with a new chief product officer and new machine-learning hires. Offensive in intent, defensive in what it concedes.
- **Q2 2026 — the tone splits.** On commerce: "Reddit's monetization engine," "$1 million revenue per employee," 43% adjusted profit margin. On users: "coming from a small base and we have a lot of work ahead of us," "our visibility in referral traffic remains low," "that work takes time to gain traction." The rhetorical register shifted from *opportunity* to *antidote* — "We are the antidote to an automated web" is a defensive metaphor, positioning Reddit against a force rather than riding one.

**Guidance specificity increased over time,** which is the right direction: by Q2 2026 the company was guiding third-quarter revenue to a tight $860–870 million band with an adjusted profit margin of 45% at the midpoint. That is not the language of a team hiding anything.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Score: High.**

The track record is unusually clean for a company two years past its listing:

- The 40% adjusted profit-margin target set at the 2024 listing was delivered in Q3 2025 and has since been exceeded (43% in Q2 2026, guided to 45% for Q3 2026).
- Eight consecutive quarters of 60%-plus revenue growth, each one landing above the prior quarter's implied expectation.
- Q2 2026 revenue of $805M came in roughly $75M — about 10% — above the ~$730M the street expected, with earnings of $1.25 per share against a $0.99 estimate.
- The screener's own record shows beats in six of the last seven quarters.

**Is there sandbagging?** Yes, mild and consistent. Reddit guides to a number it is confident of clearing, then clears it by high single digits to low double digits. That is a deliberate, healthy pattern and it means the Q3 2026 guide of $860–870 million should be read as a floor rather than a stretch.

**The one credibility debit is disclosure, not delivery.** Announcing in February 2026 that logged-in versus logged-out reporting would be phased out "later this year," and then reporting a first sequential U.S. daily-user decline in July 2026, is unfortunate sequencing. The stated rationale — that instant personalization "blurs the line between these states" — is plausible on its face. But retiring a user-quality metric in the same year the user funnel deteriorates is exactly the pattern that costs management the benefit of the doubt later. Watch whether any further user disclosure is retired in the next two calls.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The question asked in every single call, and never fully answered: what happens to Reddit when Google changes how search works?**

- *Q2 2025* — an analyst asked directly how AI mode affects traffic. Huffman: "as long as the Reddit Corpus continues to grow, users will continue to seek it out by name... I think that's created kind of a net opportunity for us." No numbers.
- *Q1 2026* — Justin Post of Bank of America asked about Google's April algorithm change. Huffman: "these things are business as usual for us. There are always puts and takes... They almost never stand out on our traffic long term. So we saw some changes in the quarter, but nothing further to comment on." That answer aged badly in exactly one quarter.
- *Q2 2026* — the same risk arrived as fact. Jason Helfstein of Oppenheimer had to ask management to justify the shape of the miss: "while you may be hurt by referral traffic, that is a high-quality user worth... multiples." Huffman accepted the framing gratefully: "I think you've got it exactly right."

That progression — deflection, then dismissal, then acceptance — is the clearest forensic finding in this dossier. **The analysts were right and management was wrong for four consecutive quarters on the single most important input to the business.**

**A second, quieter pressure point: data licensing.** Benjamin Black of Deutsche Bank asked in Q1 2026 what would move Reddit "from 2 partners to maybe 3 to 4 data licensing partners." Huffman answered in terms of "citations, mind share... general partnership" — everything except price and duration. Licensing revenue sits inside "Other Revenue," which was $140M of $2.2B in fiscal 2025 (6%) and roughly $43M in Q2 2026. For a company whose entire bull narrative rests on owning a scarce corpus, that is a strikingly small number, and management has never given the street a contract-renewal calendar.

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing:** the arithmetic of a business whose revenue grows 61% while its users grow 18% and its U.S. users shrink. Nobody on the calls has forced management to say how many quarters of revenue-per-user expansion remain.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **First sequential decline in U.S. daily users** (Q2 2026: 53.2M from 53.5M) — the first crack in five quarters, and it appeared in the shareholder letter rather than the prepared remarks.

🔴 **Four quarters of dismissing the Google risk before conceding it** (Q2 2025 through Q1 2026 "business as usual" versus Q2 2026 "choppy... more volatile"). Management's judgement on their own distribution channel was demonstrably poor.

🔴 **A user-quality disclosure retired in the year the funnel weakened** (announced Q4 2025, "phase out reporting on logged-in and logged-out later this year").

🔴 **The goal inflated as the base shrank** — "100 million daily U.S. users" (Q1 2026) became "1 billion daily users globally and 100 million in the U.S." (Q2 2026) in the quarter U.S. dailies went backwards. Undated aspiration presented as strategy.

🔴 **Stock compensation at 12% of revenue** ($338M over the last twelve months) still flatters the cash-flow headline.

🔴 **No insider has bought a share on the open market** — the screener records zero open-market purchases against 66 sales totalling 190,308 shares. Management's confidence is verbal and corporate (the buyback), not personal.

🟢 **Eight consecutive quarters above 60% revenue growth, with a profit margin rising the whole way** — Reddit is one of very few companies of any size combining 60% growth with 43% adjusted margins and a 91% gross margin.

🟢 **The 2024 listing-day margin promise was made, dated, and kept** (Q3 2025). That is the single best credibility artefact in the file.

🟢 **A genuine fortress balance sheet, verified.** As of 2026-06-30: $2.79 billion of cash and short-term investments against $20.9 million of total debt — all of it capitalized leases. Net cash of roughly $2.77 billion, about $13.69 per diluted share.

🟢 **The buyback is real and is being executed into weakness** — $234.6M repurchased in Q2 2026, with roughly $760M of the $1 billion authorization remaining and the stock now a third cheaper.

🟢 **Management disclosed the bad news themselves.** They flagged the choppy referrals and framed the user-quality trade-off rather than waiting to be caught. That is worth real credit and it is why this scores a 4 and not a 2.

🟢 **Monetization products are compounding independently of user growth** — Reddit Max advertiser count up over 60% quarter on quarter with Max revenue up over 150%; conversion volume up over 100% year over year; active advertisers up over 70%.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The metaphor changed from "oil" to "antidote."** In April 2026 Huffman called Reddit's conversations "like oil for the modern Internet, a foundational resources powering the next generation of technology" — a supplier's framing, implying pricing power over AI companies. By July 2026 the framing was "We are the antidote to an automated web" — a competitor's framing, implying Reddit is defending against AI rather than selling into it. Three months, opposite postures toward the same counterparty.

**"Drive-by traffic" is a new phrase and a load-bearing one.** It first appears in Q2 2026, twice. Reclassifying a category of users as low-value at the exact moment that category starts shrinking is a well-worn move. It happens to be *substantively defensible* here — a logged-in app user genuinely does monetize at a multiple of a search visitor — but it is still a re-definition of success delivered after the fact.

**The chief financial officer's name drifts across the transcripts** (Drew Vollero / Andrew Vollero) and the head of investor relations was mis-attributed in the Q1 2026 transcript. These are transcription artefacts, not governance events, and should not be read as turnover.

**Real leadership change did happen, and it was an admission.** A new chief product officer arrived in February 2026 alongside Huffman's statement that prior ways of working "yielded the best results we were capable of, but not the results we aspire to," plus "critical machine learning talent" hires. Management diagnosed a product-execution problem before the market did.

**Capital allocation flipped from pure reinvestment to partial return** with the February 2026 buyback, and the CFO's Q2 2026 answer on operating leverage was notably un-promotional: "There aren't huge pockets of costs that we're sort of staring at right now and say we could take that out." A company with something to hide talks about cost programmes; this one declined to.

**The unaddressed dependency.** Public reporting from 22–23 July 2026 says Reddit is weighing restricting Google's AI access to its content as the roughly $60-million-a-year licensing agreement signed in 2024 comes up for renewal, with executives reportedly wanting usage-based fees. Management did not raise this on the 30 July call and no analyst asked. That negotiation — undated, non-binding, and dependent on a counterparty that is also Reddit's largest traffic source — is the most consequential open item in the file and it is entirely absent from the transcript record.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.**

Every line that management controls is improving, and improving fast: revenue up 61%, gross margin at 91%, operating margin more than doubled year over year, free cash flow of $1.02 billion over the last twelve months against essentially zero capital spending, a $2.77 billion net-cash position, and a buyback large enough to have turned the diluted share count negative. This is not a company in trouble. It is a company whose *front door* is controlled by somebody else.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:** Reddit's revenue is compounding at 61% while its U.S. daily users just went backwards for the first time in five quarters. The entire question is whether the direct-and-app engagement work can replace search referrals *before* revenue per user runs out of room. Everything else — the margins, the balance sheet, the buyback, the licensing option — is downstream of that one race. Size the position to the possibility that the next print shows a second sequential decline, because the market has just demonstrated it will take 21% out of the stock in a single session on a beat-and-raise if the user line disappoints.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and the two halves are moving in opposite directions.**

The moat type is a **network effect wrapped in an intangible-brand asset**: roughly 100,000 active communities, more than 25 billion posts and comments accumulated over two decades, and an unpaid moderator labour force that no competitor can buy. "Reddit" being one of the most-searched words on Google is evidence that the brand, not the ranking, is what people want. Nobody is rebuilding that corpus.

The **width evidence is genuinely strong on returns**: gross margin is expanding (90.8% to 91.3% year over year), operating margin more than doubled, and because the business consumes almost no capital — $1.1 million of quarterly capital spending against $805 million of revenue — returns on the capital actually employed in operations are extraordinarily high and rising. The screener's –8% return-on-invested-capital figure is a stale artefact of the 2024 listing-year loss and should be disregarded; the current business earns very high returns on a tiny operating capital base. On the returns test alone, this moat is widening.

But a moat is a defence of the *customer relationship*, and Reddit's customer arrives through a door Google owns. The company's own chief executive is now publicly arguing that AI Overviews "has yet to make a similar level of positive impact" as the old link format. Comparable publishers have lost between a quarter and 85% of their search traffic to the same force. Reddit is far better insulated than a newspaper — it has 130 million direct daily users, its own app, and its own search product used by 80 million people weekly — but "better insulated" is narrow, not wide.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Monetization durability is widening; distribution durability is narrowing. Netting them out, the earnings base is neither obviously more nor obviously less defensible than a year ago.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is generative-AI displacement of intermediated web traffic. It is real, it is dated (it is happening now, with measurable effect), and it will compress Reddit's growth path. But it does not melt the terminal value, for two reasons the evidence supports: first, Reddit's direct user base is already large enough to carry the advertising business — revenue grew 61% in the very quarter referrals turned choppy, which is the cleanest available proof that the ad engine does not depend on drive-by traffic; second, the same force that is taking Reddit's referrals is what makes Reddit's corpus scarce, and the licensing option is a genuine, if small and unpriced, offset.

**Fear-print or value trap?** Neither cleanly, and the director should resist the temptation to call it a fear-print just because the stock fell 21% in a day and sits half off its high. On the numbers that matter — roughly nine times enterprise value to trailing revenue, about twenty times the 2027 consensus earnings estimate, and around twenty-eight times trailing free cash flow — Reddit is priced as a good growth business at a fair price, not as a distressed one. It is a **quality franchise that has de-rated to reasonable, not to cheap.** The forensic file is clean; the price is the problem.
